conceptTag: Bezos leaves a hedge fund to sell books online
readerTitle: Why Bezos walked away from his bonus to sell books online
caseNote: 실제 기업 (D. E. Shaw, Amazon 창업 결정, 1994) + 가상 적용 (가정용 전기 시공 창업)
insight: 좋은 장기 결정은 용기의 문제가 아니다. 실패해도 회복할 수 있는지, 기회의 창이 닫히고 있는지, 시도하지 않은 후회가 더 큰지를 함께 따지는 일이다.
misconception: 안정된 자리를 버리고 창업하는 것은 무모한 도박이고, 성공한 사람은 위험을 무시할 만큼 대담했을 뿐이다.

sources.text: Jeff Bezos interview, Academy of Achievement (2001): D. E. Shaw role, web growth figure, walk with David Shaw, the regret test
Brad Stone (2013). The Everything Store: Jeff Bezos and the Age of Amazon. Little, Brown: drive to Seattle, garage start, choice of books
Amazon.com 1997 Letter to Shareholders (long-term thinking, launch in July 1995)
Amazon.com press release, January 2002: first net profit, Q4 2001

factChecks.note: 웹 사용 증가율은 Bezos 본인이 여러 인터뷰에서 '연 2,300%'로 말한 수치입니다. 독립적으로 검증된 통계가 아니므로 카드에는 'more than 2,000% a year'와 'he later said'로만 적었습니다.
David Shaw와 센트럴파크를 걸으며 '좋은 직장이 없는 사람에게 더 좋은 아이디어'라는 말을 들었고 48시간 생각해 보라는 권유를 받았다는 내용은 Bezos 본인의 회고입니다. 직접 인용 대신 풀어 쓴 표현으로 적었습니다.
연중에 퇴사해 그해 보너스를 포기했다는 내용은 Bezos의 Academy of Achievement 인터뷰 등에서 본인이 말한 것입니다. 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
초기 투자자들에게 '돈을 잃을 확률이 약 70%'라고 말했다는 내용은 Bezos가 여러 인터뷰에서 반복한 회고입니다. 원문 표현과 출처를 확인하세요.
Amazon의 첫 분기 순이익은 2001년 4분기입니다(2002년 1월 발표). 연간 첫 흑자는 2003년입니다. 카드에는 'late 2001'로 적었습니다.
아내 MacKenzie가 운전하는 동안 Bezos가 사업계획서를 썼다는 내용과 Bellevue 차고 창업은 Stone(2013) 등에 나옵니다. 카드에는 출발지 없이 'drove to Seattle'로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Why Bezos walked away from his bonus to sell books online
body: In 1994, Jeff Bezos was a senior vice president at D. E. Shaw, a respected New York investment firm. He had a well-paid job and a strong career ahead.
Then he read that use of the web was growing by more than 2,000% a year. He wanted to start an online bookstore. Leaving in the middle of the year meant giving up that year's bonus.

image.label: A man at an office desk looking at a tiny glowing web browser
image.brief: 1994년 뉴욕 금융회사 사무실. 정장 차림의 남자가 책상 앞에서 작은 브라운관 모니터 속 단순한 웹페이지를 보고 있음. 창밖은 맨해튼 빌딩. 실제 회사 로고와 상표는 쓰지 않음. 인물은 특정인을 닮지 않게 단순화.

cards.title: You're in his seat.
body: You hold a senior job at a top firm. You have an idea for a business on a technology almost nobody uses yet, but its use is exploding. Your boss says it's a good idea, maybe better for someone without a great job already.

options.text: Stay until year-end, collect the bonus, then decide
options.feedback: You protect a large, certain payment. You give up months in a market where early movers may set the rules.

options.text: Keep the job and build the business on nights and weekends
options.feedback: You keep your income and your safety net. But a fast-moving market may reward the founder who is all in.

options.text: Leave now and give the idea your full attention
options.feedback: You get speed and focus. You lose the bonus and the comfort of a steady salary, with no proof the idea works.

choice.afterReveal: Bezos left mid-year and gave up the bonus. The interesting part is how he decided.

cards.title: A walk, 48 hours, then a drive west.
body: Bezos told his boss, David Shaw. By Bezos's own account, they went for a long walk in Central Park. Shaw said the idea was good, but better suited to someone without a good job. He asked Bezos to think for 48 hours.
Bezos chose books because there were millions of titles in print. No physical store could stock them all, but a website could list them.
He quit, drove to Seattle and started in a garage. Amazon opened as an online bookstore in July 1995.

cards.title: Picture yourself at 80.
body: Bezos later described what he called a **regret minimization** test. He imagined himself at 80, looking back on his life.
Would he regret trying and failing? No. He'd be proud he tried. Would he regret never trying, if the internet turned out to be huge? Yes, and that regret would stay with him.
Seen from 80, the missed bonus looked small. Seen from inside the year, it looked big.

image.label: An older man looking back along a long road at a younger self
image.brief: 긴 길 한쪽 끝에 80세 노인이 서서 뒤를 돌아보고, 멀리 반대편 끝에 젊은 시절의 자신이 갈림길 앞에 서 있음. 갈림길 표지판에는 "Stay", "Try". 따뜻한 색감의 단순한 일러스트. 실제 인물을 닮지 않게.

cards.title: Four parts of the bet.
body: The regret test worked because the rest of the bet was lopsided. Losing was survivable. Winning could be enormous. And waiting had a real cost.

breakdown.label: If it failed
breakdown.detail: A skilled finance and tech worker could find another good job

breakdown.label: If it worked
breakdown.detail: A store that could carry every book, early in a new market

breakdown.label: The window
breakdown.detail: Web use was growing fast, and others would move in

cards.softwareNote: The same four questions apply to quitting to build an app: Can you get hired again if it fails? How big is the upside? Is the window closing? What do you give up by starting now instead of next year?

cards.title: He expected to probably fail.
body: Bezos has said he told early investors there was roughly a 70% chance they would lose their money. He wasn't betting that success was likely. He was betting that the attempt was worth it.
He also planned for a long road. Amazon did not report its first quarterly profit until late 2001, more than six years after launch. A long time horizon was part of the plan, not an accident.

cards.title: We only hear this story because it worked.
body: Many people left good jobs in the 1990s to start web businesses, and most of those businesses failed. Their stories rarely get told. That's **survivorship bias**: judging a choice only by the winners.

The regret test also has a condition. It fits when failure is painful but recoverable. If failing would cost your family's home or your health, imagined regret at 80 is not a reason to jump. Check the downside first.

cards.title: Now it's an electrician.
body: You're a senior electrician at a large contractor, with a good salary. Demand for home EV chargers and solar wiring in your area is rising fast, and few small firms specialize in it yet.
You want to start your own home-services business. What's the strongest move?

options.text: Quit tomorrow and figure out clients as you go
options.feedback: You catch the window, but with no savings or first clients, one slow quarter could end the business and your finances.

options.text: Line up a few first clients, save enough to cover about a year, keep your license and contacts, then leave
options.feedback: You still move while demand is rising, and you make failure recoverable. If it doesn't work, you can return to a job.

options.text: Wait five years until it feels safe
options.feedback: You keep your income, but by then established firms may own the market. It is also the choice you're most likely to regret.

cards.title: Make the downside survivable, then ask what you'd regret.
body: Bezos's leap looked bold. Underneath, it had a recoverable downside, a huge upside and a closing window. The regret test only made the call clearer.
**Try it today:** take one decision you keep postponing. Write what happens if it fails, what happens if it works, and what waiting a year costs you.
